claims.text: Adding 1–2 at.% lanthanum to a high-entropy alloy will introduce lattice distortions.
Lanthanum is a large-lattice-parameter element suitable for inducing lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
Lanthanum-induced lattice distortions will reduce phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intervention applies to near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys having an FCC or BCC structure.
The intervention is the addition of 1–2 at.% lanthanum.
The hypothesis is intended to hold from 300 to 1000 K in polycrystalline alloys with grain size greater than 1 micrometre.
The large atomic radius of lanthanum causes lattice distortions in the alloy.
Lanthanum-induced lattice distortions increase phonon scattering.
Increased scattering from lattice distortions reduces the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path decreases phonon thermal conductivity.
The lanthanum-containing alloy will have 10–20% lower phonon thermal conductivity than the untreated alloy.
The comparison alloy should have the same processing history as the lanthanum-containing alloy but contain no added lanthanum.
The magnitude of the conductivity reduction may depend on alloy composition and processing history.
Lanthanum addition may affect strength or corrosion resistance.
Failure to observe at least a 5% conductivity reduction, or failure to detect lattice distortion, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having the same composition while also lacking the added lanthanum. Addition of 1–2 at.% lanthanum necessarily changes the composition unless 'same composition' is intended to mean the same host-element ratios after renormalization.

The prediction is a 10–20% reduction, but only a reduction below 5% is declared falsifying. A measured reduction from 5% to less than 10% would fall outside the predicted range without falsifying the stated hypothesis.
